claim: Multielectrode arrays and large silicon probes have been developed to record simultaneously between hundreds and thousands of electrodes packed with a high density.
source: In recent years, multielectrode arrays and large silicon probes have been developed to record simultaneously between hundreds and thousands of electrodes packed with a high density.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact about recent technological developments in the field.

claim: Large-scale multielectrode arrays require novel methods to extract the spiking activity of large ensembles of neurons.
source: However, they require novel methods to extract the spiking activity of large ensembles of neurons.
evidence: This is presented as a logical consequence of the technological development mentioned.

claim: The authors developed a new toolbox to sort spikes from large-scale extracellular data.
source: Here, we developed a new toolbox to sort spikes from these large-scale extracellular data.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the authors' contribution.

claim: The authors performed simultaneous extracellular and loose patch recordings in rodents to obtain ground truth data.
source: To validate our method, we performed simultaneous extracellular and loose patch recordings in rodents to obtain 'ground truth' data, where the solution to this sorting problem is known for one cell.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used for validation.

claim: The performance of the algorithm was always close to the best expected performance over a broad range of signal-to-noise ratios, in vitro and in vivo.
source: The performance of our algorithm was always close to the best expected performance, over a broad range of signal-to-noise ratios, in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the experimental results.

claim: The algorithm is entirely parallelized.
source: The algorithm is entirely parallelized and has been successfully tested on recordings with up to 4225 electrodes.
evidence: This is a statement about the computational design of the algorithm.

claim: The algorithm has been successfully tested on recordings with up to 4225 electrodes.
source: The algorithm is entirely parallelized and has been successfully tested on recordings with up to 4225 electrodes.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the testing scope of the algorithm.

claim: The toolbox offers a generic solution to sort accurately spikes for up to thousands of electrodes.
source: Our toolbox thus offers a generic solution to sort accurately spikes for up to thousands of electrodes.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the capability of the toolbox.

claim: Local circuits represent information using large populations of neurons throughout the brain.
source: As local circuits represent information using large populations of neurons throughout the brain (Buzsáki, 2010), technologies to record hundreds or thousands of them are therefore essential.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Buzsáki, 2010.

claim: Technologies to record hundreds or thousands of neurons are essential.
source: As local circuits represent information using large populations of neurons throughout the brain (Buzsáki, 2010), technologies to record hundreds or thousands of them are therefore essential.
evidence: This is presented as a logical inference from the previous statement about local circuits.

claim: Extracellular electrophysiology is one of the most powerful and widespread techniques for neuronal population recording.
source: One of the most powerful and widespread techniques for neuronal population recording is extracellular electrophysiology.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Newly developed microelectrode arrays have allowed recording of local voltage from hundreds to thousands of extracellular sites separated only by tens of microns.
source: Recently, newly developed microelectrode arrays (MEA) have allowed recording of local voltage from hundreds to thousands of extracellular sites separated only by tens of microns (Berdondini et al., 2005; Fiscella et al., 2012; Lambacher et al., 2004), giving indirect access to large neural ensembles with a high spatial resolution.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: High-density microelectrode arrays give indirect access to large neural ensembles with a high spatial resolution.
source: Recently, newly developed microelectrode arrays (MEA) have allowed recording of local voltage from hundreds to thousands of extracellular sites separated only by tens of microns (Berdondini et al., 2005; Fiscella et al., 2012; Lambacher et al., 2004), giving indirect access to large neural ensembles with a high spatial resolution.
evidence: This is presented as a consequence of the technological capability described.

claim: The spikes from a single neuron will be detected on several electrodes and produce extracellular waveforms with a characteristic spatio-temporal profile across the recording sites.
source: Thanks to this resolution, the spikes from a single neuron will be detected on several electrodes and produce extracellular waveforms with a characteristic spatio-temporal profile across the recording sites.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of high spatial resolution in recordings.

claim: Each electrode receives the activity from many neurons in high-resolution recordings.
source: However, this high resolution comes at a cost: each electrode receives the activity from many neurons.
evidence: This is presented as a trade-off of high-density recording.

claim: Spike sorting is the process of separating the waveform produced by each neuron and identifying when it appears in the recording.
source: To access the spiking activity of individual neurons, one needs to separate the waveform produced by each neuron and identify when it appears in the recording. This process, called spike sorting, has received a lot of attention for recordings with a small number of electrodes (typically, a few tens of electrodes).
evidence: This is a definition of the spike sorting process.

claim: Spike sorting has received a lot of attention for recordings with a small number of electrodes (typically, a few tens of electrodes).
source: This process, called spike sorting, has received a lot of attention for recordings with a small number of electrodes (typically, a few tens of electrodes).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the field.

claim: For large-scale and dense recordings, it is still unclear how to extract the spike contributions from extracellular recordings.
source: However, for large-scale and dense recordings, it is still unclear how to extract the spike contributions from extracellular recordings.
evidence: This is presented as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: For thousands of electrodes, the spike sorting problem is still largely unresolved.
source: In particular, for thousands of electrodes, this problem is still largely unresolved.
evidence: This is stated as a current limitation in the field.

claim: Many classical spike sorting algorithms do not take into account that the spikes of a single neuron will evoke a voltage deflection on many electrodes.
source: First, many algorithms do not take into account that the spikes of a single neuron will evoke a voltage deflection on many electrodes.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing algorithms.

claim: Most classical spike sorting algorithms do not scale up to hundreds or thousands of electrodes because their computation time would increase exponentially with the number of electrodes.
source: Second, most algorithms do not scale up to hundreds or thousands of electrodes in vitro and in vivo, because their computation time would increase exponentially with the number of electrodes (Rossant et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rossant et al., 2016.

claim: A few algorithms have been designed to process large-scale recordings.
source: A few algorithms have been designed to process large-scale recordings (Marre et al., 2012; Pillow et al., 2013; Pachitariu et al., 2016; Leibig et al., 2016; Hilgen et al., 2017; Chung et al., 2017; Jun et al., 2017), but they have not been tested on real 'ground truth' data.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Existing large-scale spike sorting algorithms have not been tested on real ground truth data.
source: A few algorithms have been designed to process large-scale recordings (Marre et al., 2012; Pillow et al., 2013; Pachitariu et al., 2016; Leibig et al., 2016; Hilgen et al., 2017; Chung et al., 2017; Jun et al., 2017), but they have not been tested on real 'ground truth' data.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing methods.

claim: Ground truth data are rare.
source: Unfortunately, such data are rare.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the availability of validation data.

claim: Dual loose patch and extracellular recordings have been performed for culture of neurons or in cortical slices.
source: Dual loose patch and extracellular recordings have been performed for culture of neurons or in cortical slices (Anastassiou et al., 2015; Franke et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In culture or slice conditions, only one or two neurons emit spikes, which simplifies the spike sorting problem drastically.
source: However, in this condition, only one or two neurons emit spikes, and this simplifies drastically the spike sorting problem.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of these experimental conditions for validation.

claim: Ground truth data recorded in vivo are scarce.
source: Ground truth data recorded in vivo are scarce (Henze et al., 2000; Neto et al., 2016) and in many cases the patch-recorded neuron is relatively far from the extracellular electrodes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In many in vivo ground truth recordings, the patch-recorded neuron is relatively far from the extracellular electrodes.
source: Ground truth data recorded in vivo are scarce (Henze et al., 2000; Neto et al., 2016) and in many cases the patch-recorded neuron is relatively far from the extracellular electrodes.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing in vivo ground truth data.

claim: Most algorithms have been tested in simulated cases where an artificial template is added at random times to an actual recording.
source: As a result, most algorithms have been tested in simulated cases where an artificial template is added at random times to an actual recording.
evidence: This is stated as common practice in the field.

claim: It is not clear if simulated data reproduce the conditions of actual recordings.
source: However, it is not clear if this simulated data reproduce the conditions of actual recordings.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of simulation-based validation.

claim: Waveforms triggered by a given neuron can vary in amplitude and shape.
source: In particular, waveforms triggered by a given neuron can vary in amplitude and shape, and most simulations do not reproduce this feature of biological data.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of biological data.

claim: Most simulations do not reproduce the variation in amplitude and shape of waveforms from biological data.
source: In particular, waveforms triggered by a given neuron can vary in amplitude and shape, and most simulations do not reproduce this feature of biological data.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing simulation approaches.

claim: Spike trains of different cells are usually correlated.
source: Also, spike trains of different cells are usually correlated, and these correlations can make extracellular spikes that do overlap.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of biological data.

claim: Correlations between spike trains can make extracellular spikes overlap.
source: Also, spike trains of different cells are usually correlated, and these correlations can make extracellular spikes that do overlap.
evidence: This is presented as a consequence of correlated spike trains.

claim: The sorting algorithm is based on a combination of density-based clustering and template matching.
source: Our sorting algorithm is based on a combination of density-based clustering and template matching.
evidence: This is a direct description of the algorithm design.

claim: The authors developed a tool automating the step that is usually left to manual curation.
source: To handle data from thousands of electrodes, we developed a tool automating the step that is usually left to manual curation.
evidence: This is a statement about a feature of the developed toolbox.

claim: The method is a fast and accurate solution for spike sorting for up to thousands of electrodes.
source: Our method is a fast and accurate solution for spike sorting for up to thousands of electrodes, and we provide it as a freely available software that can be run on multiple platforms and several computers in parallel.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the method's capabilities.

claim: The software can be run on multiple platforms and several computers in parallel.
source: Our method is a fast and accurate solution for spike sorting for up to thousands of electrodes, and we provide it as a freely available software that can be run on multiple platforms and several computers in parallel.
evidence: This is a statement about the software implementation.

claim: The ground truth data are publicly available.
source: Our ground truth data are also publicly available and will be a useful resource to benchmark future improvements in spike sorting methods.
evidence: This is a statement about data availability.

claim: The ground truth data will be a useful resource to benchmark future improvements in spike sorting methods.
source: Our ground truth data are also publicly available and will be a useful resource to benchmark future improvements in spike sorting methods.
evidence: This is a statement about the anticipated utility of the data.

claim: The algorithm has two main steps: clustering followed by template matching.
source: We developed an algorithm (called SpyKING CIRCUS) with two main steps: a clustering followed by a template matching step (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is a direct description of the algorithm structure.

claim: Spikes are detected as threshold crossings.
source: First, spikes are detected as threshold crossings (Figure 1A) and the algorithm isolated the extracellular waveforms for a number of randomly chosen spike times.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The algorithm divides snippets into groups depending on their physical positions.
source: We divided the snippets into groups, depending on their physical positions: for every electrode we grouped together all the spikes having their maximum peak on this electrode.
evidence: This is a description of the algorithm's processing strategy.

claim: The ensemble of spikes was divided into as many groups as there were electrodes.
source: Thanks to this division, the ensemble of spikes was divided into as many groups as there were electrodes.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the grouping strategy.

claim: A single cell can only influence the electrodes in its vicinity.
source: We assumed that a single cell can only influence the electrodes in its vicinity, and only kept the signal on electrodes close enough to the peak (Figure 1B, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated as an assumption of the algorithm.

claim: The simple division in groups before clustering allowed parallelization of the clustering step.
source: Note that the simple division in groups before clustering allowed us to parallelize the clustering step, making it scalable for even thousands of electrodes.
evidence: This is stated as a benefit of the algorithm design.

claim: The density-based clustering was inspired by Rodriguez and Laio, 2014.
source: For each group, we performed a density-based clustering inspired by (Rodriguez and Laio, 2014) (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The centroid of a cluster in the feature space should have many neighbours (high density of points).
source: The idea of this algorithm is that the centroid of a cluster in the feature space should have many neighbours, that is a high density of points in their neighborhood.
evidence: This is stated as the principle behind the clustering algorithm.

claim: The centroid should be the point where density is a local maximum.
source: The centroid should also be the point where this density is a local maximum: there should not be a point nearby with a higher density.
evidence: This is stated as a criterion for identifying centroids.

claim: The algorithm hypothesized a maximum of ten clusters in each group.
source: We hypothesized that there was a maximum of ten clusters in each group (i.e. at most ten different cells peaking on the same electrode) and took the ten points with the largest δ/ρ ratio as the centroids.
evidence: This is stated as a parameter choice in the algorithm.

claim: In many spike-sorting methods, it is assumed that finding clusters is enough to solve the spike-sorting problem.
source: In many spike-sorting methods, it is assumed that finding clusters is enough to solve the spike-sorting problem (Chung et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chung et al., 2017.

claim: Clustering alone neglects the specific issue of overlapping spikes.
source: However, this neglects the specific issue of overlapping spikes (see Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of clustering-only approaches.

claim: When two nearby cells spike synchronously, the extracellular waveforms evoked by each cell will superimpose.
source: When two nearby cells spike synchronously, the extracellular waveforms evoked by each cell will superimpose (Figure 1C, see also [Pillow et al., 2013]).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and illustrated in a figure.

claim: Superimposition of two signals from two different cells will distort the feature estimation.
source: This superimposition of two signals coming from two different cells will distort the feature estimation.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of signal superimposition.

claim: Overlapping spikes will appear as points very far away from the cluster associated to each cell.
source: As a result, these spikes will appear as points very far away from the cluster associated to each cell.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of feature distortion.

claim: Each template is composed of two waveforms.
source: This template is a simplified description of the cluster and is composed of two waveforms.
evidence: This is a description of the template structure.

claim: The first component of a template is the average extracellular waveform evoked by the putative cell.
source: The first one is the average extracellular waveform evoked by the putative cell (Figure 1C, left and red waveforms).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: The second component is the direction of largest variance that is orthogonal to the average waveform.
source: The second is the direction of largest variance that is orthogonal to this average waveform (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of how the second component is computed.

claim: Each waveform triggered by a cell is assumed to be a linear combination of the two template components.
source: We assumed that each waveform triggered by this cell is a linear combination of these two components.
evidence: This is stated as an assumption of the model.

claim: The algorithm is tolerant to some errors in the clustering.
source: Note that we only used the clusters to extract the templates. Our algorithm is thus tolerant to some errors in the clustering.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the algorithm design.

claim: The algorithm can tolerate errors in the delineation of the cluster border.
source: For example, it can tolerate errors in the delineation of the cluster border.
evidence: This is given as an example of the algorithm's tolerance to clustering errors.

claim: The clustering task is less demanding than in classical spike sorting algorithms where finding the correct cluster borders is essential.
source: The clustering task here is therefore less demanding than in classical spike sorting algorithms where finding the correct cluster borders is essential to minimize the final error rate.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to classical approaches.

claim: The template matching algorithm assumes that the templates of different cells spiking together sum linearly.
source: To match the templates to the data we used an iterative greedy approach to estimate the aij for each ti, which bears some similarity to the matching pursuit algorithm (Mallat and Zhifeng Zhang, 1993).
evidence: This is stated as an assumption of the template matching step.

claim: The template matching uses a greedy iterative approach inspired by the projection pursuit algorithm.
source: To match the templates to the data we used an iterative greedy approach to estimate the aij for each ti, which bears some similarity to the matching pursuit algorithm (Mallat and Zhifeng Zhang, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mallat and Zhifeng Zhang, 1993.

claim: The authors recorded 18 neurons from 14 retinas with a 252 electrode MEA where the spacing between electrodes was 30 μm.
source: In vitro, we recorded 18 neurons from 14 retinas with a 252 electrode MEA where the spacing between electrodes was 30 μm (see Materials and methods, (Spampinato et al., 2018)).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data collected.

claim: There was a correlation between the error rate of the algorithm and the size of the extracellular waveform evoked by the spikes of the patch-recorded cell.
source: Looking at Figure 2C, for in vitro data (see Materials and methods), we found that there was a correlation between the error rate of our algorithm and the size of the extracellular waveform evoked by the spikes of the patch-recorded cell: the higher the waveform, the lower the error rate.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The higher the waveform, the lower the error rate.
source: Looking at Figure 2C, for in vitro data (see Materials and methods), we found that there was a correlation between the error rate of our algorithm and the size of the extracellular waveform evoked by the spikes of the patch-recorded cell: the higher the waveform, the lower the error rate.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the data.

claim: A proxy for best possible performance can be found by training a nonlinear classifier on the ground truth data.
source: However, a proxy can be found by training a nonlinear classifier on the ground truth data (Harris et al., 2000; Rossant et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The performance of the algorithm almost always was in the same order of magnitude as the performance of the nonlinear classifier.
source: We estimated the error made by the classifier and found that the performance of our algorithm almost always was in the same order of magnitude as the performance of this classifier, (Figure 2D, left; r=0.89, p<10−5) over a broad range of spike sizes.
evidence: This is stated as a finding with statistical support (r=0.89, p<10−5).

claim: For 37 neurons with large waveform sizes, the average error of the classifier is 2.7% and the one for the algorithm is 4.8%.
source: For 37 neurons with large waveform sizes (above) the average error of the classifier is 2.7% and the one for our algorithm is 4.8% (see Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: For 22 neurons with lower spike size, the average error of the classifier is 11.1% and the one for the algorithm is 15.2%.
source: For 22 neurons with lower spike size (below), the average error of the classifier is 11.1% and the one for our algorithm is 15.2%.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data.

claim: The algorithm achieved an almost optimal performance on in vitro data.
source: This suggests that our algorithm reached an almost optimal performance on this in vitro data.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the comparison with the classifier.

claim: The algorithm achieved near optimal performance on in vivo data.
source: With the same approach as for in vitro data, we also found that our algorithm achieved near optimal performance (Figure 2F, right; r=0.92, p<10−5), although there were only two recordings where the spike size of the patch-recorded neuron was large enough to be sorted with a good accuracy.
evidence: This is stated as a finding with statistical support (r=0.92, p<10−5).

claim: For two available neurons with low optimal error rate, the average error of the classifier is 13.9% and the one for the algorithm is 14.8%.
source: For only two available neurons with low optimal error rate, the average error of the classifier is 13.9% and the one for our algorithm is 14.8%.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the in vivo data.

claim: For 24 neurons with lower spike size, the average error of the classifier is 64.0% and the one for the algorithm is 67.8%.
source: For 24 neurons with lower spike size, the average error of the classifier is 64.0% and the one for our algorithm is 67.8%.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the in vivo data.

claim: The algorithm can reach a satisfying performance over a broad range of spike sizes, for both in vivo and in vitro recordings.
source: Together, these results show that our algorithm can reach a satisfying performance (i.e. comparing to the classifier error) over a broad range of spike sizes, for both in vivo and in vitro recordings.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the results.

claim: The performance of SpyKING CIRCUS was similar to Kilosort (4.4% on average for SpyKING CIRCUS against 4.2% for Kilosort).
source: We also compared our performance to the Kilosort algorithm (Pachitariu et al., 2016) and found similar performances (4.4% on average over all non-decimated neurons for SpyKING CIRCUS against 4.2% for Kilosort).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison with another algorithm.

claim: Kilosort can achieve a four times speedup on a standard desktop machine using a GPU.
source: Because Kilosort used a GPU, it could be run faster than our algorithm on a single machine: on a 1 hr recording with 252 electrodes, Kilosort can achieve a four times speedup on a standard desktop machine (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of execution speed.

claim: Without using a GPU, Kilosort was only marginally faster (1.5 speedup).
source: But without using a GPU, Kilosort was only marginally faster (1.5 speedup), and slower if we started using several cores of the machine.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of execution speed without GPU.

claim: The speedup of Kilosort comes at the cost of an increased usage of memory.
source: However, is it worth noticing that the speedup of Kilosort comes at the cost of an increased usage of memory.
evidence: This is stated as a trade-off of Kilosort's design.

claim: Kilosort used 32 GB of RAM for a maximal number of 500 neurons.
source: Kilosort used 32 GB of RAM for a maximal number of 500 neurons, while our algorithm had a much lower memory footprint, because of design choices.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of memory usage.

claim: SpyKING CIRCUS has a much lower memory footprint than Kilosort.
source: Kilosort used 32 GB of RAM for a maximal number of 500 neurons, while our algorithm had a much lower memory footprint, because of design choices.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison of memory usage.

claim: SpyKING CIRCUS can run on recordings with thousands of electrodes while Kilosort does not scale up to this number.
source: Thanks to this, we could run our algorithm to process recordings with thousands of electrodes, while Kilosort does not scale up to this number.
evidence: This is stated as a capability difference between the two algorithms.

claim: Every step of the algorithm should be run in parallel over different CPUs to process recordings with thousands of electrodes.
source: A crucial condition to process recordings performed with thousands of electrodes is that every step of the algorithm should be run in parallel over different CPUs.
evidence: This is stated as a design requirement.

claim: The clustering step was run in parallel on different subsets of snippets.
source: The clustering step of our algorithm was run in parallel on different subsets of snippets as explained above.
evidence: This is a description of the parallelization strategy.

claim: The template matching step could be run independently on different blocks of data.
source: The template matching step could be run independently on different blocks of data, such that the computing time only scaled linearly with the data length.
evidence: This is a description of the parallelization strategy.

claim: The computing time only scaled linearly with the data length.
source: The template matching step could be run independently on different blocks of data, such that the computing time only scaled linearly with the data length.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the algorithm's scalability.

claim: The runtime of the full algorithm decreased proportionally with the numbers of CPU cores available.
source: The runtime of the full algorithm decreased proportionally with the numbers of CPU cores available (Figure 3A, grey area indicates where the software is 'real-time' or faster).
evidence: This is stated as a finding shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The sorting algorithm could process 1 hr of data recorded with 252 electrodes in 1 hr with 9 CPU cores.
source: As a result, the sorting algorithm could process 1 hr of data recorded with 252 electrodes in 1 hr with 9 CPU cores (spread over three computers) (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result about processing speed.

claim: The algorithm scaled up linearly with the number of electrodes.
source: It also scaled up linearly with the number of electrodes (Figure 3B), and with the number of templates (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The algorithm scaled up linearly with the number of templates.
source: It also scaled up linearly with the number of electrodes (Figure 3B), and with the number of templates (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated as a finding shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The total error rate remained below 5% for all the spikes whose size was significantly above spike detection threshold.
source: Summing these two types of errors, the total error rate remained below 5% for all the spikes whose size was significantly above spike detection threshold (normalized amplitude corresponds to the spike size divided by the spike threshold).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the hybrid dataset tests.

claim: Error rates were similar for recordings with 4255 electrodes in vitro, 128 electrodes in vivo or 252 electrodes in vitro.
source: Error rates were similar for recordings with 4255 electrodes in vitro, 128 electrodes in vivo or 252 electrodes in vitro.
evidence: This is stated as a finding about the consistency of performance across different recording scales.

claim: Performance did not depend on the firing rate of the injected templates.
source: Performance did not depend on the firing rate of the injected templates (Figure 3E) and only weakly on the normalized amplitude of the templates (Figure 3F), as long as it was above the spike threshold.
evidence: This is stated as a finding shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Performance only weakly depended on the normalized amplitude of the templates, as long as it was above the spike threshold.
source: Performance did not depend on the firing rate of the injected templates (Figure 3E) and only weakly on the normalized amplitude of the templates (Figure 3F), as long as it was above the spike threshold.
evidence: This is stated as a finding shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The accuracy of the algorithm is invariant to the size of the recordings.
source: The accuracy of the algorithm is therefore invariant to the size of the recordings.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the scaling tests.

claim: If an algorithm misses overlapping spikes, then the estimation of the amplitude of correlations between cells will be biased.
source: If an algorithm misses overlapping spikes, then the estimation of the amplitude of correlations between cells will be biased.
evidence: This is stated as a logical consequence.

claim: The method was able to estimate the pairwise correlation between the spike trains with no underestimation.
source: We found that our method was always able to estimate the pairwise correlation between the spike trains with no underestimation (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is stated as a finding shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Overlapping spikes were correctly detected by the algorithm.
source: Overlapping spikes were therefore correctly detected by our algorithm.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the correlation test.

claim: The ability of the template matching algorithm to resolve overlapping spikes allowed an unbiased estimation of correlations between spike trains.
source: The ability of our template matching algorithm to resolve overlapping spikes thus allowed an unbiased estimation of correlations between spike trains, even for thousands of electrodes.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the algorithm's capability.

claim: SpyKING CIRCUS reached a similar performance for 4225 electrodes than for hundreds electrodes.
source: These different tests, described above, show that SpyKING CIRCUS reached a similar performance for 4225 electrodes than for hundreds electrodes, where our ground truth recordings showed that performance was near optimal.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the scaling tests.

claim: The algorithm is able to sort accurately recordings from thousands of electrodes.
source: Our algorithm is therefore also able to sort accurately recordings from thousands of electrodes.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the validation tests.

claim: The algorithm may split one cell into several units.
source: As in most spike-sorting algorithms, our algorithm may split one cell into several units.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of spike sorting algorithms.

claim: It is necessary to merge together the units corresponding to the same cell after running the entire algorithm.
source: After running the entire algorithm, it is therefore necessary to merge together the units corresponding to the same cell.
evidence: This is stated as a necessary post-processing step.

claim: For hundreds or thousands of electrodes, going through all the pairs of units and merging them by hand would take a substantial amount of time.
source: However, for hundreds or thousands of electrodes, going through all the pairs of units and merging them by hand would take a substantial amount of time.
evidence: This is stated as a practical challenge for large-scale recordings.

claim: The authors designed a tool to merge automatically many units at once.
source: To overcome this problem, we designed a tool to merge automatically many units at once so that the time spent on this task does not scale with the number of electrodes and this allows us to automate this final step.
evidence: This is a statement about the solution developed.

claim: Units that likely belong to the same cell have templates that look alike.
source: Units that likely belong to the same cell (and thus should be merged) have templates that look alike and in addition, the combined cross-correlogram between the two cell's spike trains shows a clear dip near 0 ms, indicating that the merged spike trains do not show any refractory period violation (Figure 4A, blue example).
evidence: This is stated as a criterion for identifying units to merge.

claim: The combined cross-correlogram between two cells' spike trains that belong to the same cell shows a clear dip near 0 ms.
source: Units that likely belong to the same cell (and thus should be merged) have templates that look alike and in addition, the combined cross-correlogram between the two cell's spike trains shows a clear dip near 0 ms, indicating that the merged spike trains do not show any refractory period violation (Figure 4A, blue example).
evidence: This is stated as a criterion for identifying units to merge, illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: A dip near 0 ms in the cross-correlogram indicates that the merged spike trains do not show any refractory period violation.
source: Units that likely belong to the same cell (and thus should be merged) have templates that look alike and in addition, the combined cross-correlogram between the two cell's spike trains shows a clear dip near 0 ms, indicating that the merged spike trains do not show any refractory period violation (Figure 4A, blue example).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the cross-correlogram feature.

claim: The error rate obtained with the automated merging method was close to the best error rate obtained by merging using ground truth data for guidance.
source: We found that the error rate obtained with our automated method was close to this best error rate (Figure 4C).
